u1-w1.title: Find the work people do together
u1-w1.task: Read Working Together. Put its main idea in the center of a web, then add three details that show how people cooperate. Add the page number beside every detail.
u1-w1.check: The main idea covers the whole selection, and each branch is evidence rather than an opinion.

u1-w1.title: Trace what Election Day makes possible
u1-w1.task: Read Election Day. Build a three-link chain showing an action, what it causes, and the result. Include one graphic feature that helped you understand the sequence.
u1-w1.check: Every arrow can be defended with words or a graphic from the selection.

u1-w1.title: Compare two ways people participate
u1-w1.task: Place the important events from both selections on two parallel timelines. Circle one similarity in how people work together and explain one important difference.
u1-w1.check: Both timelines stay in text order and the comparison uses evidence from both selections.

u1-w1.title: Write to someone about civic participation
u1-w1.task: Use the official weekly writing focus to draft a personal letter explaining one useful way people can participate in a community. Support the letter with one detail from each selection.
u1-w1.check: The letter has a clear audience, an organized message, two sourced details, and an edited closing.

u1-w1.title: Read and sort short-vowel words
u1-w1.task: Read Robert's Rules of Order. Collect words that show the week’s short-vowel pattern, sort them by vowel sound, and use two collected words in a summary of the selection.
u1-w1.check: Each word is copied accurately, sorted by its sound, and used in a sentence that matches the text.

u1-w2.title: Build a precise summary of a right
u1-w2.task: Read It Is My Right! Identify who wanted change, the obstacle, the response, and the result. Turn those notes into a concise summary.
u1-w2.check: The summary includes only essential events and keeps them in a logical order.

u1-w2.title: Connect actions to consequences
u1-w2.task: Reread It Is My Right! Record three cause-and-effect relationships. For each one, quote or closely paraphrase the sentence that proves the connection.
u1-w2.check: Each effect follows from the stated cause and includes a page reference.

u1-w2.title: Infer how ideas influence change
u1-w2.task: Read Thomas Paine, then compare it with It Is My Right! Infer one way ideas can influence public action and support the inference with evidence from both texts.
u1-w2.check: The inference goes beyond a copied fact but remains supported by both selections.

u1-w2.title: Explain how change happens
u1-w2.task: Follow the official informative-writing focus to explain how people or ideas can help secure a right. Organize evidence from both selections into related points before drafting.
u1-w2.check: The explanation has a focused introduction, grouped evidence, linking words, and a conclusion.

u1-w2.title: Use long-a patterns in context
u1-w2.task: Reread Thomas Paine. Find examples of the week’s long-a spellings, place them under VCe, ai, ay, or a, and write a text-based sentence with one word from two different columns.
u1-w2.check: The spelling categories are accurate and both sentences make sense in the selection’s context.

u1-w3.title: Name the central idea about voting rights
u1-w3.task: Read Winning the Right to Vote. State the main idea, list four supporting details, and rank the details from strongest to weakest support.
u1-w3.check: The top-ranked detail directly explains the main idea, not merely the topic.

u1-w3.title: Reconstruct the sequence of change
u1-w3.task: Reread Winning the Right to Vote. Build a timeline of major developments and attach one text or graphic clue to every event.
u1-w3.check: Events are ordered correctly and every annotation explains why that event matters.

u1-w3.title: Connect voting rights to a diverse nation
u1-w3.task: Read One Nation from Many. Compare how the two selections develop the idea of participation in a nation, including one contribution made by a graphic feature.
u1-w3.check: The matrix contains evidence from both texts and distinguishes text evidence from graphic evidence.

u1-w3.title: Take a position on civic participation
u1-w3.task: Use the official opinion-writing focus to state which form of participation described this week is most important. Give reasons and evidence from both selections, then address one possible disagreement.
u1-w3.check: The opinion is unmistakable, reasons are linked to evidence, and the ending follows from the argument.

u1-w3.title: Distinguish long-o and long-u spellings
u1-w3.task: Reread One Nation from Many. Make cards for words with the week’s long-o and long-u patterns, mark the letters producing each sound, and use selected cards to explain one key detail.
u1-w3.check: Sound-spelling marks are accurate and the explanation remains faithful to the text.

u2-w1.title: Track choice and consequence in two fables
u2-w1.task: Read both Aesop fables in the selection. For each, record the character’s choice, immediate consequence, and final outcome, then write a one-sentence summary.
u2-w1.check: Each summary identifies the decisive event without retelling every detail.

u2-w1.title: Notice how a ballad builds a hero
u2-w1.task: Read the two famous poems. Identify repeated sound, rhythm, exaggeration, or story-like features that make each a ballad and cite a short example for every feature.
u2-w1.check: Every named genre feature is connected to visible language in the poems.

u2-w1.title: Compare characters across forms
u2-w1.task: Choose one character from the fables and one from the ballads. Record a trait for each, evidence for each trait, and one shared quality in the center.
u2-w1.check: Traits are inferred from actions or words, not selected without evidence.

u2-w1.title: Create a fable with a proven lesson
u2-w1.task: Use the official fable-writing process. Borrow a structural move—not wording—from one Aesop fable: a character wants something, makes a revealing choice, faces a consequence, and exposes a lesson.
u2-w1.check: The lesson grows naturally from the character’s choice and the draft has been revised and edited.

u2-w1.title: Apply long-e patterns to a folktale
u2-w1.task: Read Geese for the Queen. Sort long-e words by spelling pattern, then use three of the words in a short note explaining what one character does.
u2-w1.check: The collected words carry the long-e sound and the note describes an event from the folktale accurately.

u2-w2.title: Reduce the Midas myth to essential events
u2-w2.task: Read The Tale of King Midas. Select only five events needed to understand the problem, turning point, and resolution; caption each in your own words.
u2-w2.check: Removing any chosen event would make the myth’s cause-and-effect chain harder to understand.

u2-w2.title: Prove how a trait drives the plot
u2-w2.task: Reread the Midas myth. Name one trait, cite the action that reveals it, and trace two later events caused by that action.
u2-w2.check: The chain shows how character—not coincidence—moves the story forward.

u2-w2.title: Compare two Greek heroes’ choices
u2-w2.task: Read Theseus and the Minotaur. Compare Midas and Theseus by the choice each makes, the motive behind it, and its consequence.
u2-w2.check: Each comparison point cites the correct myth and avoids mixing story events.

u2-w2.title: Explain how character creates consequence
u2-w2.task: Use the official explanatory-writing focus to explain how a major trait shapes the outcome in one myth. Plan a claim, sequence evidence, and explain the connection after each detail.
u2-w2.check: The explanation tells why the evidence matters instead of listing events.

u2-w2.title: Use long-i words to capture the challenge
u2-w2.task: Reread Theseus and the Minotaur. Sort long-i words by pattern, then write a two-sentence précis of the central challenge using two collected words naturally.
u2-w2.check: Patterns are accurate and the précis includes the challenge and response.

u2-w3.title: Summarize the folktale’s turning points
u2-w3.task: Read Snow White: A Russian Folktale. Mark the beginning situation, two turning points, and resolution, then use the path to write a compact summary.
u2-w3.check: The summary explains change across the story and does not become a scene-by-scene retell.

u2-w3.title: Read mood through words and illustrations
u2-w3.task: Choose two moments from Snow White. For each, pair one illustration detail with one phrase from the text and explain how together they establish mood.
u2-w3.check: Mood words are precise and both visual and verbal evidence support them.

u2-w3.title: Compare an ordinary and outsized character
u2-w3.task: Read Paul Bunyan’s Big Thirst. Compare a central character from each selection through problem, response, and defining trait; note how folktale and tall-tale conventions differ.
u2-w3.check: The comparison includes evidence and identifies a meaningful genre difference.

u2-w3.title: Write a supported review
u2-w3.task: Follow the official opinion-review process to recommend one selection to another Grade 3 reader. Give criteria, cite examples, and explain why the examples meet the criteria.
u2-w3.check: The review evaluates rather than summarizes and includes a clear recommendation.

u2-w3.title: Build compound words from the tall tale
u2-w3.task: Reread Paul Bunyan’s Big Thirst. Find compound words, divide each into meaningful parts, define it from context, and use one to describe the tall-tale exaggeration.
u2-w3.check: Both word parts are real words and the context definition fits the sentence.

u3-w1.title: Explain how disguise supports survival
u3-w1.task: Read Animal Disguises. State the main idea on a shield shape and place three details around it that show how disguise protects an animal.
u3-w1.check: Each detail explains survival and supports one complete main idea.

u3-w1.title: Use photographs and charts as evidence
u3-w1.task: Read Animals’ Tools for Survival. Make three pairs: one fact from the words and one fact from a photograph or chart that deepens the same idea.
u3-w1.check: The graphic evidence adds information instead of merely repeating a caption.

u3-w1.title: Compare two kinds of adaptation
u3-w1.task: Compare one disguise with one survival tool. Record what each structure or behavior does, how they are alike, and how they solve different problems.
u3-w1.check: The comparison names specific adaptations from both texts and their functions.

u3-w1.title: Launch a focused adaptation inquiry
u3-w1.task: Use the official research focus to form one answerable question about an adaptation introduced this week. Gather relevant notes from both selections and mark which text supplied each note.
u3-w1.check: The question is neither too broad nor already answered by one copied sentence, and every note is sourced.

u3-w1.title: Hear r-controlled vowels in shark facts
u3-w1.task: Read The Remarkable Teeth of a Shark. Sort words by /är/ and /ôr/, mark the controlling r, and use two words in an explanation of how shark teeth function.
u3-w1.check: Sounds are sorted accurately and the explanation is supported by the selection.

u3-w2.title: Determine what body coverings accomplish
u3-w2.task: Read Fur, Skin, Scales, or Feathers. Write the main idea, group supporting details by body covering, and identify which group provides the strongest support.
u3-w2.check: Groups are logical and every detail supports the overall main idea.

u3-w2.title: Separate reasons from evidence
u3-w2.task: Reread the selection. Record three claims or reasons about body coverings and the precise evidence the author provides for each.
u3-w2.check: Evidence is a fact or example from the text, not a restatement of the reason.

u3-w2.title: Compare protection strategies
u3-w2.task: Read Caterpillar Self-Defense. Compare a caterpillar defense with one body-covering adaptation, using text and graphic evidence to explain how each protects an animal.
u3-w2.check: The matrix names the strategy, evidence, and protective result for both animals.

u3-w2.title: Evaluate sources for an animal question
u3-w2.task: Choose one adaptation question from this week. Use the official research focus to record what each selection contributes, what it does not answer, and what kind of additional source would be useful.
u3-w2.check: The notes distinguish available evidence from missing information and justify the next source type.

u3-w2.title: Apply er, ir, and ur to self-defense
u3-w2.task: Reread Caterpillar Self-Defense. Sort words by er, ir, and ur spellings, then write a short defense explanation that accurately uses three sorted words.
u3-w2.check: Each word belongs in its spelling column and the explanation states a real defense from the text.

u3-w3.title: Synthesize many adaptations into one idea
u3-w3.task: Read One Body, Many Adaptations. Connect the main idea to at least four adaptations, labeling how each helps the animal meet a need.
u3-w3.check: Every connection names both the adaptation and the need it addresses.

u3-w3.title: Trace evidence through cause and effect
u3-w3.task: Choose three adaptations from the selection. For each, identify the author’s evidence and infer the survival effect that evidence supports.
u3-w3.check: Inferences follow logically from cited evidence and are labeled as inferences.

u3-w3.title: Separate scientific explanation from pourquoi tale
u3-w3.task: Read How the Chameleon Learned to Change Color. Compare how the informational text and pourquoi tale explain adaptation, including purpose, evidence, and genre conventions.
u3-w3.check: The comparison does not treat a fictional explanation as scientific fact.

u3-w3.title: Audit authorship before taking notes
u3-w3.task: Use the official research focus to identify author, genre, purpose, and evidence type for both selections. Decide which is appropriate for a factual adaptation claim and explain why.
u3-w3.check: The decision is based on source purpose and evidence, not preference.

u3-w3.title: Decode closed syllables in a pourquoi tale
u3-w3.task: Reread the chameleon tale. Collect closed-syllable words, divide multisyllabic examples, mark short vowels, and use selected words to recount the tale’s explanation.
u3-w3.check: Syllable divisions preserve pronounceable parts and the recount stays faithful to the tale.

u4-w1.title: Summarize Cinderella’s day from her record
u4-w1.task: Read Cinderella’s Very Bad Day. Select the entries or events that cause the largest changes and arrange them into a beginning–middle–end summary.
u4-w1.check: The summary reflects the diary’s event order and omits minor repetition.

u4-w1.title: Read point of view through drama
u4-w1.task: Read Cinderella, Too Much for Words. Track what two speakers say and what the stage directions reveal, then explain whose point of view becomes clearest.
u4-w1.check: The explanation distinguishes spoken dialogue from stage directions and cites both.

u4-w1.title: Compare how Cinderella stories frame events
u4-w1.task: Compare one shared kind of event through the diary and play. Record how each narrator or speaker frames it and identify any idiom or hyperbole that changes the tone.
u4-w1.check: The chart compares viewpoints rather than merely listing plot differences.

u4-w1.title: Write a controlled point-of-view comparison
u4-w1.task: Follow the official essay focus: choose a basis for comparison, organize similarities and differences, quote accurately, link ideas, and conclude what the viewpoints change for the reader.
u4-w1.check: The organization is consistent and every quotation is followed by explanation.

u4-w1.title: Find open syllables in another folktale
u4-w1.task: Read Cap o’ Rushes. Divide selected multisyllabic words, identify open syllables, and use three words in a note describing one character’s point of view.
u4-w1.check: Marked syllables end in a vowel sound and the viewpoint note is text-based.

u4-w2.title: Choose the events Jack’s story cannot lose
u4-w2.task: Read Jack and the Beanstalk. List six major events, then remove one and explain whether the story still makes sense; use the test to create a summary.
u4-w2.check: The final summary preserves the central conflict, key choices, and outcome.

u4-w2.title: Separate reader and character viewpoints
u4-w2.task: For one major event, record what Jack knows, what another character knows, and what you as the reader know. Explain how the differences shape your judgment.
u4-w2.check: Each column uses information actually available to that viewpoint at that moment.

u4-w2.title: Hear the giant’s side
u4-w2.task: Read The Giant’s Complaint. Identify the giant’s strongest complaint, compare it with Jack’s actions in the fairy tale, and decide where the viewpoints genuinely conflict.
u4-w2.check: Both positions receive fair text evidence before the decision is made.

u4-w2.title: Dramatize a viewpoint conflict
u4-w2.task: Use the official play-writing focus to create a scene in which Jack and the giant argue about one event. Add stage directions that reveal feelings the dialogue does not state directly.
u4-w2.check: Voices stay distinct, stage directions are playable, and the scene has a clear turn.

u4-w2.title: Use consonant-le words in the giant’s case
u4-w2.task: Reread The Giant’s Complaint. Find and divide consonant-le words, then use two of them in a statement presenting the giant’s claim and evidence.
u4-w2.check: Syllables are divided correctly and the evidence statement represents the text accurately.

u4-w3.title: Map a play’s decisive moments
u4-w3.task: Read The True Jack? For each scene, write the event that changes what a character thinks or does; combine only those changes into a summary.
u4-w3.check: The summary follows the drama’s scenes and emphasizes decisions over stage business.

u4-w3.title: Explain how an illustration positions the reader
u4-w3.task: Choose an illustration from The True Jack? Annotate details that create mood or favor a point of view, then connect each annotation to a moment in the text.
u4-w3.check: Annotations describe visible details and explain their effect rather than naming mood alone.

u4-w3.title: Compare drama with science fiction
u4-w3.task: Read The Beanstalk Experiment. Compare how the play and science-fiction selection use the beanstalk idea, focusing on narrator/speaker, evidence, and reader experience.
u4-w3.check: The chart identifies how form changes meaning, not only how plots differ.

u4-w3.title: Argue which account is more convincing
u4-w3.task: Use the official opinion focus to choose which selection offers the more convincing version of the beanstalk idea. Organize reasons, cite both sources, and respond to the strongest opposing reason.
u4-w3.check: The judgment uses criteria and evidence from both sources.

u4-w3.title: Read vowel-team syllables in science fiction
u4-w3.task: Reread The Beanstalk Experiment. Divide words containing vowel-team syllables, underline each team, and use three words to explain the experiment described.
u4-w3.check: Teams remain together when divided and the explanation does not add unreported results.

u5-w1.title: Explain Bell’s central achievement
u5-w1.task: Read Alexander Graham Bell: “It Talks!” State the main idea and choose three details that show the problem, Bell’s work, and the result.
u5-w1.check: The details form a coherent path from need to achievement.

u5-w1.title: Track how communication technology changes
u5-w1.task: Read From Telephone to FaceTime! Build a timeline of changes and annotate how the author’s choice of examples serves the text’s purpose.
u5-w1.check: The timeline is sequential and the purpose claim is supported by the selected examples.

u5-w1.title: Compare invention story and technology history
u5-w1.task: Compare how the biography and technology overview teach the telephone topic. Include text features, author purpose, and one fact each source contributes uniquely.
u5-w1.check: The comparison distinguishes biography from broad historical explanation.

u5-w1.title: Narrate a moment of technological change
u5-w1.task: Use the official narrative focus to write from the viewpoint of someone experiencing an early communication technology. Ground the scene in facts from both selections while creating dialogue and sensory detail.
u5-w1.check: Invented narration does not contradict source facts and point of view remains consistent.

u5-w1.title: Mark VCe syllables in a wire story
u5-w1.task: Read The Longest Wire. Collect words with Vowel-Consonant-e syllables, mark the pattern, and use two words in a cause-and-effect statement about the wire.
u5-w1.check: The silent-e pattern is marked correctly and the statement is supported by the selection.

u5-w2.title: Distill Edison’s biography
u5-w2.task: Read Thomas Edison: “It Sings!” Identify the challenge, actions, achievement, and significance, then turn the frame into a concise summary.
u5-w2.check: The summary explains significance instead of ending with a disconnected fact.

u5-w2.title: Follow the sequence the author selected
u5-w2.task: Reread the Edison biography. Map the order of key events and explain why this order helps the author present Edison’s work.
u5-w2.check: The explanation connects sequence to purpose with specific event evidence.

u5-w2.title: Compare two technology biographies
u5-w2.task: Read George Eastman and the Kodak Camera. Build parallel timelines for Edison and Eastman and identify one shared innovation pattern and one difference.
u5-w2.check: Both timelines are text-based and the comparison follows from their sequence.

u5-w2.title: Explain an innovation process
u5-w2.task: Use the official informational focus to explain how one inventor moved from problem to usable technology. Combine sequence with another useful structure such as cause/effect or comparison.
u5-w2.check: The organization is visible, facts are sourced, and illustrations or labels clarify rather than decorate.

u5-w2.title: Read vowel-r syllables in camera history
u5-w2.task: Reread the Eastman selection. Divide words containing vowel-r syllables, label the vowel-r unit, and use three cards to summarize one stage of camera development.
u5-w2.check: Divisions are accurate and the summary follows the published account.

u5-w3.title: Identify the idea behind changing music formats
u5-w3.task: Read From Phonograph to Playlist. State the main idea and arrange supporting details to show how the technology develops over time.
u5-w3.check: Every detail advances the same main idea and is placed in correct sequence.

u5-w3.title: Separate causes, effects, and sequence
u5-w3.task: Reread the selection. Mark which relationships are chronological and which are cause/effect; explain how the two structures work together.
u5-w3.check: Examples are correctly classified and the explanation refers to both structures.

u5-w3.title: Compare two paths from old to new
u5-w3.task: Read From Snapshots to Selfies. Compare the development of recorded sound and photography, including one inference about why each technology changed.
u5-w3.check: Inferences are grounded in details from the correct selection.

u5-w3.title: Defend the more significant advancement
u5-w3.task: Use the official opinion focus to decide which advancement had the larger effect on everyday life. Establish criteria, organize evidence from both texts, and maintain an authoritative tone.
u5-w3.check: The conclusion follows the stated criteria, not personal preference alone.

u5-w3.title: Use -ed and -ing to describe change
u5-w3.task: Reread From Snapshots to Selfies. Collect base words with -ed or -ing, note spelling changes, and revise a three-sentence technology summary to use the forms accurately.
u5-w3.check: Base words and spelling changes are correct and verb tense stays consistent.

u6-w1.title: Track the decision that changes each folktale
u6-w1.task: Read The Fox and the Geese. Identify the crucial decision, what follows, and how the story ends; use those elements in a compact summary.
u6-w1.check: The summary makes the decision’s consequence clear.

u6-w1.title: Prove a trait through action
u6-w1.task: Read The Three Spinsters. Choose one character trait, cite two actions that reveal it, and explain how the actions shape the problem or solution.
u6-w1.check: The trait is inferred from behavior and both actions affect the story.

u6-w1.title: Compare lessons across two Grimm tales
u6-w1.task: State the lesson of each folktale and connect it to a character’s decision. Then explain the strongest similarity or difference between the lessons.
u6-w1.check: Each lesson is supported by events and is stated as a general idea, not plot summary.

u6-w1.title: Paraphrase before researching
u6-w1.task: Use the official research focus to take one direct quotation and one paraphrased note from each folktale about decision-making. Label them and explain which form is more useful for a comparison.
u6-w1.check: Paraphrases change both wording and structure without changing meaning; quotations are exact.

u6-w1.title: Use irregular plurals in a factual text
u6-w1.task: Read The Incredible Goose. Find irregular plurals or related singular/plural pairs, record the change, and use them in two accurate science facts from the selection.
u6-w1.check: Number agreement is correct and both facts come from the text.

u6-w2.title: Summarize Doctor Knowall through decisions
u6-w2.task: Read Doctor Knowall. Select the decisions that create the problem, turn the action, and lead to the ending; use only those points in a synopsis.
u6-w2.check: The synopsis is chronological and excludes entertaining but nonessential details.

u6-w2.title: Track what the character knows and chooses
u6-w2.task: For three moments in Doctor Knowall, record what the central character believes, what action follows, and what the reader can infer.
u6-w2.check: Beliefs, actions, and reader inferences remain distinct.

u6-w2.title: Compare how two folktales judge choices
u6-w2.task: Read The Kid and the Wolf. Place a major choice from each story on a wise-to-foolish scale and defend each placement with consequences from the texts.
u6-w2.check: The judgment uses consequences as evidence and represents both stories accurately.

u6-w2.title: Search for evidence without losing source identity
u6-w2.task: Use the official research focus to gather notes answering: How do folktales teach about decisions? Paraphrase evidence, include one exact quotation, and tag every note by title.
u6-w2.check: Every note can be traced to a source and directly addresses the question.

u6-w2.title: Distinguish long and short oo
u6-w2.task: Reread The Kid and the Wolf. Sort words by long-oo and short-oo sound, verify each in context, and use one from each group in a warning the character might learn.
u6-w2.check: Sorting follows pronunciation, and the warning matches the folktale’s outcome.

u6-w3.title: Identify the chain of choices in the folktale
u6-w3.task: Read The Wolf and the Fox. Record each major choice and consequence, then condense the chain into a summary centered on the characters’ decisions.
u6-w3.check: The summary retains the causal chain and final outcome.

u6-w3.title: Derive the message from actions
u6-w3.task: Choose three actions from The Wolf and the Fox. Explain what each reveals and use the pattern to state the central message.
u6-w3.check: The message is a transferable lesson supported by all three actions.

u6-w3.title: Compare fictional canines with scientific information
u6-w3.task: Read Canine Cousins: The Fox and the Wolf. Compare how the folktale portrays the animals with what the science text explains, separating character invention from factual information.
u6-w3.check: No fictional trait is presented as scientific evidence.

u6-w3.title: Evaluate evidence for a fox-and-wolf question
u6-w3.task: Use the official research focus to form a question about foxes and wolves, rank notes from both selections by usefulness, and explain which source can support factual claims.
u6-w3.check: The ranking considers genre, relevance, and accuracy.

u6-w3.title: Hear /ou/ in canine facts
u6-w3.task: Reread Canine Cousins. Collect words with /ou/ as in how and out, mark the spelling, and use selected words in a two-fact synthesis.
u6-w3.check: Words carry the target sound and both facts are supported by the informational text.

u7-w1.title: Identify how the writer views a community
u7-w1.task: Read Exploring My Community. State the main idea and collect three words, details, or choices that reveal the author’s point of view.
u7-w1.check: The viewpoint claim is supported by the author’s language, not assumed from the topic.

u7-w1.title: Infer how a new place affects a character
u7-w1.task: Read A New Life in Vermont. Record three character actions, infer what each reveals about adjustment to the community, and summarize the change across the story.
u7-w1.check: Each inference is plausible from the cited action and the summary shows development.

u7-w1.title: Compare a personal and fictional community experience
u7-w1.task: Compare what each selection teaches about joining or exploring a community. Include one illustration detail and explain how it shapes understanding.
u7-w1.check: The comparison uses both texts and explains, rather than merely names, the visual contribution.

u7-w1.title: Compare communities with disciplined organization
u7-w1.task: Follow the official writing focus to compare the communities or experiences. Choose subject-by-subject or point-by-point organization, avoid first person, link facts, and conclude from evidence.
u7-w1.check: The selected structure stays consistent and facts from both sources are balanced.

u7-w1.title: Use -er and -or in community roles
u7-w1.task: Read The Mission District. Find words ending in -er or -or, identify the base and the person or thing named, and use two words in a fact about the community.
u7-w1.check: Suffix meanings are accurate and the fact is grounded in the text.

u7-w2.title: Organize the kinds of communities
u7-w2.task: Read All Kinds of Communities. State the main idea, sort key details into meaningful categories, and label how each category supports the idea.
u7-w2.check: Categories do not overlap unnecessarily and every detail contributes to the whole.

u7-w2.title: Read maps, photos, and captions together
u7-w2.task: Select a map, photo, and caption from the selection. Record what each adds and how the combination influences the author’s presentation of communities.
u7-w2.check: Each note identifies information available from the feature, not just its appearance.

u7-w2.title: Compare broad community types with one historic place
u7-w2.task: Read The Levi Coffin House. Compare the broad discussion of communities with this specific place, identifying what the second text makes more concrete.
u7-w2.check: Evidence from both texts supports the general-to-specific relationship.

u7-w2.title: Create a narrative rooted in place
u7-w2.task: Use the official narrative focus to write a scene in one sourced community setting. Develop characters through action and varied dialogue attribution without changing documented place facts.
u7-w2.check: Setting facts remain accurate, dialogue moves the scene, and characters are developed through choices.

u7-w2.title: Resolve homophones through context
u7-w2.task: Reread The Levi Coffin House. Build homophone pairs from target words, write a context clue for each correct spelling, and use one pair in two contrasting sentences about the text.
u7-w2.check: Each sentence’s meaning proves the chosen spelling.

u7-w3.title: Summarize a historical-fiction problem
u7-w3.task: Read Sarah and the Chickens. Identify the historical setting, central problem, character response, and outcome; combine them into a summary.
u7-w3.check: The summary distinguishes setting information from story events.

u7-w3.title: Use illustrations to read historical setting
u7-w3.task: Choose an illustration and related passage. Annotate details that establish time, place, or daily life and explain how they support the historical-fiction genre.
u7-w3.check: Every annotation connects a visible or textual detail to historical setting.

u7-w3.title: Compare imagined history with remembered history
u7-w3.task: Read Wind and Wildflowers. Compare how character action in historical fiction and remembered experience in memoir reveal life in a community.
u7-w3.check: The comparison respects each genre and cites both selections.

u7-w3.title: Argue from multiple community sources
u7-w3.task: Use the official opinion focus to decide which selection gives a reader a stronger sense of community life. Link reasons to evidence from both sources and revise the conclusion to follow the argument.
u7-w3.check: The essay evaluates using stated criteria and includes evidence from both genres.

u7-w3.title: Study variant /ô/ in memoir
u7-w3.task: Reread Wind and Wildflowers. Collect words representing variant spellings of /ô/, group them by spelling, and use two in a memoir-detail synthesis.
u7-w3.check: Words share the target sound and the synthesis reports remembered details accurately.

u8-w1.title: Read weather through poetic images
u8-w1.task: Read Fairweather Clouds. Mark images, comparisons, or line choices that shape the weather experience and explain what each helps the reader imagine.
u8-w1.check: Explanations connect exact poetic language to meaning rather than paraphrasing the whole poem.

u8-w1.title: Build the main idea from weather features
u8-w1.task: Read Earth’s Weather and Climate. State the main idea and attach details from headings, diagrams, captions, or descriptions that develop it.
u8-w1.check: Each feature contributes information and supports the same main idea.

u8-w1.title: Compare experiencing weather with explaining it
u8-w1.task: Compare how the poem and informational text represent weather. Include language, evidence, and the experience each form gives the reader.
u8-w1.check: The comparison explains the effect of form, not just a topic similarity.

u8-w1.title: Form a researchable weather question
u8-w1.task: Use the official research focus to turn one weather curiosity into a focused question. List what each selection contributes and identify an additional print or online source type needed.
u8-w1.check: The question invites investigation, and source choices are justified by the information needed.

u8-w1.title: Distinguish hard and soft c in storm facts
u8-w1.task: Read Blizzard Alert! Sort c words by sound, infer the spelling condition for each, and use selected words in an accurate explanation of a blizzard detail.
u8-w1.check: Sound groups and inferred rules match the collected examples.

u8-w2.title: Trace change across Water Sky
u8-w2.task: Read Water Sky. Identify the initiating situation, key responses, turning point, and outcome, then summarize how the situation changes.
u8-w2.check: The summary explains change and preserves event order.

u8-w2.title: Test realistic-fiction features
u8-w2.task: Reread Water Sky. Record setting, characters, events, and text features that make the story realistic, noting which details are plausible rather than proven facts.
u8-w2.check: The chart distinguishes realistic invention from informational evidence.

u8-w2.title: Compare realistic and traditional weather stories
u8-w2.task: Read How Indian Summer Began. Compare how realistic fiction and a pourquoi tale use weather, focusing on purpose, explanation, and evidence.
u8-w2.check: The comparison does not present the pourquoi explanation as scientific fact.

u8-w2.title: Plan a researched weather narrative
u8-w2.task: Use the official research-and-narrative focus to take notes on an authentic weather condition, choose a viewpoint, and plan a story event that remains consistent with the facts.
u8-w2.check: Research notes are sourced and the planned event does not contradict them.

u8-w2.title: Apply hard and soft g to a tale
u8-w2.task: Reread How Indian Summer Began. Sort g words by sound, mark the letters that follow g, and use two cards to recount the tale’s explanation.
u8-w2.check: Pronunciations and spellings are correct and the recount stays within the tale.

u8-w3.title: Explain the tropical rain belt’s main idea
u8-w3.task: Read The Tropical Rain Belt. State the main idea and place key details by location or condition to show how they support it.
u8-w3.check: Map labels are drawn from the text and together explain the central idea.

u8-w3.title: Integrate graphics with description
u8-w3.task: Match three graphic elements to the paragraphs they clarify. Explain what information becomes easier to understand when each pair is read together.
u8-w3.check: The explanation identifies a specific contribution from both graphic and prose.

u8-w3.title: Compare climate description with prediction
u8-w3.task: Read Predicting Hurricanes. Compare how each text uses data or graphics, then make one inference about weather knowledge supported by both.
u8-w3.check: The inference is labeled and supported by evidence from both selections.

u8-w3.title: Write a factual firsthand weather account
u8-w3.task: Use the official firsthand-account focus to narrate observing a weather event. Incorporate accurate research, temporal language, and a closing that follows the experience.
u8-w3.check: First-person details may be created, but all weather claims remain supported by the sources.

u8-w3.title: Hear diphthongs in hurricane information
u8-w3.task: Reread Predicting Hurricanes. Collect diphthong words, group them by sound and spelling, and use three to explain one prediction method.
u8-w3.check: Sound-spelling groups are accurate and the method is represented faithfully.

u9-w1.title: Connect choices to ideas in two short texts
u9-w1.task: Read both parts of Making Choices. Identify the central idea or lesson in each and connect it to the detail or event that best supports it.
u9-w1.check: The informational idea and fable lesson are stated in forms appropriate to each genre.

u9-w1.title: Trace the farmers’ market process
u9-w1.task: Read Let It Grow. Sequence the steps or operations described, identify any proverb or key phrase, and explain how the procedure supports the author’s purpose.
u9-w1.check: Steps are ordered and the purpose statement is supported by the process described.

u9-w1.title: Compare practical and literary lessons about choices
u9-w1.task: Compare what the informational and literary texts teach about choices involving time or resources. Record how each genre supports its message.
u9-w1.check: The chart uses evidence from both forms and does not flatten them into the same genre.

u9-w1.title: Design a research path for a spending choice
u9-w1.task: Use the official research focus to choose a focused question about spending time or money. Write subquestions and categorize the kinds of sources that could answer each.
u9-w1.check: Each source category has a clear purpose and the question is manageable.

u9-w1.title: Use dis- and un- to revise meaning
u9-w1.task: Read The Milkmaid. Find or build text-relevant words with dis- and un-, show how each prefix changes the base meaning, and use two in a lesson statement.
u9-w1.check: Base meanings are accurate and the lesson statement fits the folktale.

u9-w2.title: Summarize the choices that define Lazy Harry
u9-w2.task: Read Lazy Harry. Select the choices that create, worsen, and resolve the problem, then summarize without unrelated episodes.
u9-w2.check: The summary links actions to consequences and reaches the outcome.

u9-w2.title: Interpret idiom and illustration together
u9-w2.task: Choose an idiom and an illustration detail from Lazy Harry. Explain each in context and show how both contribute to understanding the character.
u9-w2.check: The idiom is interpreted figuratively and the illustration claim names visible evidence.

u9-w2.title: Test a theme across two foolish choices
u9-w2.task: Read Two Foolish Brothers. Propose a theme shared with Lazy Harry, then test it against two events from each story and revise it if any event does not fit.
u9-w2.check: The final theme is general, defensible across both texts, and supported by four events.

u9-w2.title: Explain a folktale lesson with credited evidence
u9-w2.task: Use the official informational focus to explain what the two folktales teach about decision-making. Organize around main ideas, quote and credit each source, and conclude with the shared significance.
u9-w2.check: Source credit is clear and each quotation is analyzed.

u9-w2.title: Use pre- and re- to change time or repetition
u9-w2.task: Reread Two Foolish Brothers. Analyze words with pre- and re- or build relevant examples, then place them on a before/again timeline and use two in a text-based statement.
u9-w2.check: Prefix meanings are accurate and the statement reflects an event or lesson.

u9-w3.title: Follow fruit from choice to product
u9-w3.task: Read From Fruit to Jam. State the main idea and arrange key details along the process or choice sequence that develops it.
u9-w3.check: The ladder maintains order and every rung supports the main idea.

u9-w3.title: Explain what sidebars add
u9-w3.task: Compare information in the main text and sidebars. Explain how each serves the author’s purpose and identify one connection a reader must make.
u9-w3.check: The chart identifies distinct contributions instead of restating both sections.

u9-w3.title: Compare producer and consumer viewpoints
u9-w3.task: Read Where Do You Get Your Produce? Place both authors’ viewpoints on an evidence line and explain similarities or differences using language and details from each.
u9-w3.check: Viewpoint claims are tied to author choices, not assumed from titles.

u9-w3.title: Plan an interview that fills an evidence gap
u9-w3.task: Use the official research focus to identify an unanswered produce question, draft purposeful interview questions, distinguish essential from interesting information, and plan how to quote the source.
u9-w3.check: Questions are open enough to yield evidence and directly address the identified gap.

u9-w3.title: Use -able, -ful, and -less precisely
u9-w3.task: Reread Where Do You Get Your Produce? Analyze or build topic-relevant words with -able, -ful, and -less, define each from its parts, and use them to compare two produce choices.
u9-w3.check: Suffix meanings are preserved and the comparison remains factual.

u10-w1.title: Explain movement through poetic language
u10-w1.task: Read both Poems of Movement. Mark rhyme, rhythm, and image choices that create movement, then explain the different experience each poem gives.
u10-w1.check: Each explanation connects a named poetic feature to its effect.

u10-w1.title: Identify how a procedure explains motion
u10-w1.task: Read What Makes Things Move? Sequence the procedure or investigation, then connect its steps and results to the text’s main idea.
u10-w1.check: The sequence is complete enough to show how evidence supports the idea.

u10-w1.title: Compare feeling movement with investigating it
u10-w1.task: Compare reading the poems with reading the science text. Record what each lets the reader notice about movement and how language or evidence creates that effect.
u10-w1.check: The comparison describes reader experience and supports it with features from both texts.

u10-w1.title: Build an evidence-based force opinion
u10-w1.task: Use the official research focus to choose a force or motion question, gather facts, and state a provisional opinion with reasons. Mark what further evidence would strengthen it.
u10-w1.check: Facts are sourced, reasons support the opinion, and missing evidence is identified honestly.

u10-w1.title: Break apart compound words in a fable
u10-w1.task: Read The Tortoise and the Hare. Divide compound words into bases, define them, and use selected words to explain how a character’s movement affects the outcome.
u10-w1.check: Both bases contribute to meaning and the outcome explanation matches the fable.

u10-w2.title: Summarize the struggle in the tug-of-war
u10-w2.task: Read The Great Tug-of-War. Identify the conflict, attempts, turning point, and resolution, then write a summary focused on how the struggle changes.
u10-w2.check: The summary includes essential events and makes the resolution clear.

u10-w2.title: Rank words by force and intensity
u10-w2.task: Collect verbs or descriptions related to force and movement. Arrange them from weaker to stronger and explain how one image affects the scene.
u10-w2.check: The scale reflects contextual meaning and the imagery explanation cites exact language.

u10-w2.title: Infer a lesson across two fables
u10-w2.task: Read The Merchant’s Donkey. Build a bridge from evidence in each selection to one inference about effort, resistance, or choice; note where the texts differ.
u10-w2.check: Both evidence sets support the inference and the difference is not ignored.

u10-w2.title: Research and answer an opposing reason
u10-w2.task: Use the official opinion-research focus to state a claim about a choice in the texts, support reasons with evidence, identify an opposing view, and plan a fair response.
u10-w2.check: The response addresses the opposing reason itself rather than dismissing it.

u10-w2.title: Build abstract nouns with -ment and -ness
u10-w2.task: Reread The Merchant’s Donkey. Analyze words with -ment and -ness or build relevant examples, define the abstract nouns, and use two to express the fable’s lesson.
u10-w2.check: Base-to-suffix changes are accurate and the lesson is supported by events.

u10-w3.title: Identify what the magnetism investigation shows
u10-w3.task: Read Investigate: Magnetism. State the investigation question, record key evidence or observations, and explain the main idea the evidence supports.
u10-w3.check: The main idea follows from the recorded investigation evidence.

u10-w3.title: Read across procedure and other text formats
u10-w3.task: Identify the procedure, labels, graphics, sidebars, or other formats in the selection. Explain the job each performs and how the parts work together.
u10-w3.check: Every format is linked to a specific information function.

u10-w3.title: Integrate magnetism information from two texts
u10-w3.task: Read Why Didn’t I Think of That? Combine nonduplicate facts from both texts into one labeled explanation of magnetism or its use, marking each source.
u10-w3.check: The model credits each fact and does not add an unsupported mechanism.

u10-w3.title: Defend a useful application with evidence
u10-w3.task: Use the official opinion focus to choose the most useful application or investigation idea from the texts. State reasons, link evidence, respond to an alternative, and conclude.
u10-w3.check: The opinion uses scientific information accurately and the response treats the alternative fairly.

u10-w3.title: Connect related words to scientific meaning
u10-w3.task: Reread Why Didn’t I Think of That? Build families of related words, identify shared bases and meaning changes, and use members from two families in a sourced explanation.
u10-w3.check: Relationships are morphological or semantic, and the explanation is supported by the text.
